title: AppArmor Profile Violation Detection
exclusions: This use case reports indexed records containing the modern AppArmor blocked-access signature `apparmor="DENIED"`. It does not alert on `apparmor="ALLOWED"`: AppArmor documents that tag for implicit violations admitted by complain mode, while audit/force-audit settings can also increase logging of allowed operations; a complain-mode learning report therefore requires a separately validated profile-mode inventory. It excludes profile load, replace, remove, status, error, and hint messages; generic Linux DAC failures; non-AppArmor AVCs; unconfined processes; and denials that AppArmor, auditd, printk rate limiting, collection filters, or transport did not record or deliver. A result does not prove malicious intent, compromise, successful exploitation, the process's final outcome, current profile mode, policy correctness, fleet confinement coverage, or regulatory compliance. The search does not author, reload, relax, disable, or switch profiles and contains no default allowlist or suppression lookup.
evidence: After deployment, retain the version-controlled `linux_apparmor_denied` saved-search definition and ACL, scheduler dispatch and alert-action history, result rows, the matching raw AppArmor records and audit IDs, effective forwarder `inputs.conf`/`props.conf`, source-selection decision, `aa-status` output, applicable module/profile audit-mode output, profile file and local-override hashes, and dated positive/negative control results. Record every threshold, routing, and suppression approval with owner and expiry. These artifacts show only what the configured log path delivered and what the search classified; this documentation-only review does not claim that a saved search, dashboard, evidence index, retention policy, production validation, or complete fleet coverage already exists.

controlTest.positiveScenario: In an isolated test index and one searched source type, index a current-bucket record with `host=apparmor-positive` and raw payload `type=AVC msg=audit(1761678000.100:501): apparmor="DENIED" operation="open" class="file" profile="/usr/sbin/exampled" name="/srv/restricted" pid=4242 comm="exampled" requested_mask="r" denied_mask="r" fsuid=1000 ouid=0`. Set `_time` inside the closed five-minute result bucket selected by the scheduled search. Expect exactly one row with `aa_profile=/usr/sbin/exampled`, `aa_operation=open`, `aa_class=file`, `aa_comm=exampled`, `aa_denied_mask=r`, `denied_records=1`, `distinct_audit_ids=1`, `threshold_policy=any_logged_denial`, and `severity=medium`.
controlTest.negativeScenario: Using the same host, fields, and time window, replace the decision with `apparmor="ALLOWED"` and expect no row; this is the required complain/allowed guard. Also verify that an AppArmor profile-load/status message without the exact decision, a generic `type=SYSCALL ... success=no` record, and a non-AppArmor AVC produce no rows. Place a valid DENIED record outside the closed time bounds and expect no row. Finally, omit `profile`, `operation`, or `name` one at a time from a DENIED fixture and confirm the event remains visible under `not_recorded` rather than disappearing during aggregation.

dataSources: AppArmor kernel audit records delivered through exactly one canonical path per host into the deployment-selected `index=os`: (1) `/var/log/audit/audit.log` as `sourcetype=linux_audit`, (2) Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux `rlog.sh`/ausearch output as `sourcetype=auditd`, or (3) the kernel facility in `/var/log/syslog`, `/var/log/kern.log`, or `/var/log/messages` as `sourcetype=syslog`. A Splunk journald input is also viable when it preserves the audit message in `MESSAGE` and explicitly assigns one of the searched source types. The required source contract is `_time`, `host`, `_raw`, and an event body containing the exact quoted key/value decision `apparmor="DENIED"`; common optional AppArmor fields include `operation`, `class`, `profile` or `label`, `name`, `comm`, `requested_mask`, and `denied_mask`. Do not enable audit-file, kernel-log, and journald collection simultaneously for the same host without a proved deduplication design.
app: Splunk Add-on for Unix and Linux (`Splunk_TA_nix`, Splunkbase 833) for its documented `linux_audit`/`auditd` source-type knowledge and Linux forwarder deployment; a native Splunk Universal Forwarder file monitor or journald input can supply the kernel-log alternative. No premium Splunk app is required.

spl:
index=os earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m (sourcetype=linux_audit OR sourcetype=auditd OR sourcetype=syslog) apparmor DENIED
| eval event_text=coalesce(MESSAGE,_raw)
| rex field=event_text "apparmor=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_decision>[A-Z_]+)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| where aa_decision="DENIED"
| rex field=event_text "type=(?<aa_record_type>AVC|USER_AVC|1400|1107)"
| rex field=event_text "audit\((?<aa_audit_id>\d+(?:\.\d+)?:\d+)\)"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)operation=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_operation>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)class=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_class>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)profile=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_profile>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)label=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_label>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)name=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_name>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)comm=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_comm>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)requested_mask=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_requested_mask>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| rex field=event_text "(?:^|\s)denied_mask=(?:\x5c)?\x22(?<aa_denied_mask>.*?)(?:\x5c)?\x22"
| eval aa_profile=coalesce(aa_profile,aa_label,"not_recorded"), aa_record_type=coalesce(aa_record_type,"not_recorded"), aa_operation=coalesce(aa_operation,"not_recorded"), aa_class=coalesce(aa_class,"not_recorded"), aa_name=coalesce(aa_name,"not_recorded"), aa_comm=coalesce(aa_comm,"not_recorded"), aa_requested_mask=coalesce(aa_requested_mask,"not_recorded"), aa_denied_mask=coalesce(aa_denied_mask,"not_recorded")
| stats count AS denied_records dc(aa_audit_id) AS distinct_audit_ids values(aa_audit_id) AS audit_ids values(aa_name) AS target_names earliest(_time) AS first_seen_epoch latest(_time) AS last_seen_epoch BY host aa_profile aa_operation aa_class aa_comm aa_requested_mask aa_denied_mask
| where denied_records>=1
| eval threshold_policy="any_logged_denial", severity="medium"
| table last_seen_epoch first_seen_epoch host severity threshold_policy denied_records distinct_audit_ids aa_profile aa_operation aa_class aa_comm aa_requested_mask aa_denied_mask target_names audit_ids
| sort 0 -denied_records host aa_profile aa_operation
description: Detects AppArmor access attempts that the indexed kernel audit record explicitly marks `apparmor="DENIED"`, extracts the documented policy context, and groups blocked records by host, profile or label, operation, class, command, and masks over one completed five-minute bucket. It intentionally separates enforced denials from complain-mode or force-audit `ALLOWED` activity and returns the first logged denial rather than waiting for an unsupported universal count.
value: A logged AppArmor denial can reveal a legitimate application/profile mismatch, a failed deployment, unexpected runtime behavior, or an attempted action outside an enforced policy boundary. Preserving the exact decision, profile, operation, object, command, masks, and audit identity shortens service-impact and security triage without treating every generic kernel or audit failure as an AppArmor violation.
implementation: Choose one authoritative AppArmor event path for each host, preserve the original key/value record, verify the exact `apparmor="DENIED"` signature, and schedule the SPL every five minutes over its closed delayed bucket. Trigger when result count is greater than zero and start with medium-severity ticketing; there is no AppArmor, Linux-kernel, or Splunk source supporting the previous `count>5` boundary. Validate normal volume and service context before changing routing. Keep complain-mode `ALLOWED` learning activity in a separate report tied to measured profile mode, and never suppress source ingestion or raw evidence.
visualization: Use a current-findings table keyed by `host`, `aa_profile`, and `aa_operation`, showing decision count, distinct audit IDs, class, command, requested/denied masks, target names, and first/last epoch. Add a stacked timechart of `denied_records` by profile and operation plus a separate collection-freshness/profile-coverage panel. Label counts as indexed AppArmor DENIED records per completed five-minute bucket, not attacks, blocked processes, affected users, or unique incidents. Drill down to the matching raw record and on-host profile state; protect object paths and command details as security telemetry.
dataModelAcceleration: Not applicable. Splunk CIM does not publish an accelerated data-model contract for AppArmor decision, profile/label, operation, class, requested mask, denied mask, and audit identity. The primary search therefore validates and extracts the raw AppArmor record. A `tstats` variant requires a separately governed local data model and parity tests against raw results.

knownFalsePositives:
Every matched record should be a real indexed AppArmor `DENIED` decision. A "false positive" here means an expected block, duplicated collection, a policy-development artifact, or routing that overstates the event—not a fabricated denial.

1. **Approved negative or policy regression test** — Security engineering may deliberately request a forbidden file, capability, network action, or execution transition to prove confinement. Confirm the exact host, profile, operation, object, test owner, ticket, and bounded UTC window. Retain the result as control evidence; mute only notification delivery for that exact test scope.

2. **Application upgrade or packaging change** — A new binary path, library/cache location, helper process, socket, capability, or systemd behavior can conflict with an otherwise legitimate profile. Correlate package-manager and deployment records, service logs, profile source/version, local includes, and rollback state. The denial is genuine and may cause service impact; do not label an upgrade as benign until the owner confirms the requested behavior is intended.

3. **Profile authoring or complain-to-enforce transition** — A profile moved into enforce mode before learning is complete can produce a burst of genuine denials. Compare dated `aa-status`, deployment automation, parser/reload logs, profile hash, and change record. Restore the approved profile state or add the narrow reviewed rule; do not disable AppArmor or broadly allow a path from the alert alone.

4. **Intentional explicit deny** — Policy may deliberately deny a noisy probe, optional feature, or unsafe path. AppArmor documentation notes that explicit deny rules can quiet denials unless audit is requested, so any visible record is still evidence of a blocked request. Route known audited denies to a lower-priority report only when the profile owner has documented why recurrence is expected and why retaining visibility is necessary.

5. **Duplicate ingestion paths** — Monitoring `audit.log` while also ingesting the same kernel record through syslog or journald can inflate `denied_records`. Compare `audit_ids`, source, sourcetype, `_indextime`, and forwarder identity. Choose one canonical path; do not rely on count tuning to hide duplicate architecture.

6. **Shared or misleading host metadata** — Cloned forwarder configuration or host rewriting can attribute a valid denial to the wrong asset. Compare the Splunk forwarder GUID, source host, audit serial, CMDB identity, and same-time on-host log before changing policy.

7. **Missing extraction fields** — Some mediation classes use `label` instead of `profile`, omit `name`, or carry class-specific fields. The SPL keeps the denial under `not_recorded`; this is not automatically an unknown-profile attack. Inspect the complete raw record and qualify parser behavior for that kernel/AppArmor version.

**Safe suppression:** the base SPL has no exception lookup because no repository artifact establishes one. If local governance requires suppression, apply it after exact-signature detection with a reviewed lookup keyed at minimum by host, exact profile, operation, and where stable the target/class, plus `valid_from_epoch`, `valid_until_epoch`, owner, ticket, and reason. Reject permanent, wildcard-profile, host-wide, or missing-expiry rows. Preserve source records and detection results, test expiry, and review the exception whenever the profile, package, kernel, AppArmor parser, or service owner changes.
mitreAttack: N/A (a blocked AppArmor policy action does not by itself establish an adversary technique)

cost.search_load_notes: Scheduled raw-event filter and bounded rex/stats processing over one delayed ten-to-five-minute bucket; actual load depends on AppArmor audit volume and duplicated collection paths.

reviewer: Cursor AI documentation-only editorial review against AppArmor, Linux kernel, and Splunk primary documentation; no Splunk runtime, distribution matrix, production profile, control fixture, security SME, or service-owner validation
detailedImplementation:
## Prerequisites and detection boundary

Assign a Linux/AppArmor owner, a Splunk content owner, and service owners for the confined profiles. Confirm that the kernel has AppArmor enabled, policy is loaded, and the applications in scope are actually confined. The Linux kernel documentation is explicit that tasks without a loaded profile run unconfined; an empty denial search therefore cannot prove protection. Run `aa-status` under approved privilege and retain its enforce, complain, kill where supported, and unconfined counts. Also inspect the applicable module or policy-namespace audit setting and profile source. AppArmor can quiet denials, explicit deny rules may be quiet unless combined with audit, auditd or printk can drop messages under pressure, and collection can filter them. Treat coverage and log-pipeline health as separate controls.

Understand the decision tags before deploying. AppArmor documents `apparmor="DENIED"` for a policy access that enforcement rejected. Kill mode is an enforcement variant that also signals the task, but the record used here is not sufficient to prove whether a task was killed or remained alive. In complain mode an implicit policy violation is allowed and logged as `apparmor="ALLOWED"`; complain mode is for learning and does not provide the same enforcement. Explicit deny and stacked-policy behavior can still reject operations in cases where complain mode does not convert them. The independent audit/force-audit flag increases logging of allowed and denied actions. For these reasons, this alert accepts only `DENIED`, names it a blocked policy action, and makes no current-mode inference from the event alone. Build a separate `ALLOWED` learning report only after joining a dated, authoritative profile-mode inventory and testing audit-mode behavior on each supported AppArmor/kernel line.

AppArmor uses the kernel audit subsystem but does not require the auditd userspace daemon. With auditd, records normally reach `/var/log/audit/audit.log`; without it they can reach the kernel ring buffer and then `/var/log/kern.log`, `/var/log/messages`, `/var/log/syslog`, or journald according to distribution logging. Modern examples use `type=AVC` or numeric `type=1400`; userspace-mediated records can use `USER_AVC` or `1107`. The stable detection signature is the quoted `apparmor="DENIED"` key/value, not the word `denied` alone and not a generic AVC type.

## Step 1 — Configure data collection through exactly one ingestion path

Inventory the real source on each distribution with `journalctl -k --grep='apparmor='`, the configured audit log, and kernel log files. Choose one path per host class. Do not monitor the same event in audit.log, syslog, and journald concurrently. If auditd writes the complete key/value record, use the add-on's documented `linux_audit` file source type or its `rlog.sh`/ausearch `auditd` output after proving that translation preserves every field needed by this rule. If auditd is absent, monitor the one distribution-specific kernel log that actually receives the record and assign `sourcetype=syslog`. `index=os` is a catalogue convention, not a Splunk default; replace it consistently in the search and input.

A minimal direct audit-file monitor is:

```ini
[monitor:///var/log/audit/audit.log]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = linux_audit
```

A kernel-log host might instead deploy one, and only one, stanza such as:

```ini
[monitor:///var/log/kern.log]
disabled = 0
index = os
sourcetype = syslog
```

Use `/var/log/syslog` or `/var/log/messages` only when that is the actual destination. Broadly monitoring `/var/log` through an add-on and adding another local stanza can duplicate data. Inspect effective configuration with `splunk btool inputs list --debug`, search by `host source sourcetype`, and compare audit IDs before rollout.

For a journald-only host, Splunk's documented journald input can collect kernel messages and preserves `MESSAGE` as a required field. Start with a simple reviewed stanza, use `journalctl-dmesg` and a supported `journalctl-grep` only after checking the installed `journalctl` version, explicitly set index and sourcetype, and verify the indexed event shape. The SPL uses `coalesce(MESSAGE,_raw)` so a structured journal event can expose the unescaped message. Do not assume a default sourcetype or copy a filter across old systemd versions: Splunk documents field/filter version differences and duplicate output when identical journald stanzas run.

The forwarder account needs only the access required to read the chosen source. Do not grant policy-write, profile-reload, or broad root capability merely for collection. Protect audit data in transit and restrict search access because `name`, `comm`, labels, paths, capabilities, and peer details can expose sensitive service structure. Measure event volume and retention under local policy rather than inventing a fixed daily ingest estimate.

## Step 2 — Create the search and alert after verifying parsing

Capture representative raw records for file, capability, network, mount, signal, ptrace, D-Bus, and namespaced/container mediation that actually occur in scope. Confirm `_time` follows event time, `host` identifies the originating machine, and `_raw` or `MESSAGE` retains `apparmor="DENIED"`. AppArmor fields vary by mediation class. Standard file examples contain `operation`, `profile`, `name`, `pid`, `comm`, `requested_mask`, and `denied_mask`; userspace records may use `label` and peer-specific fields. The SPL therefore normalizes `profile` then `label`, preserves absent dimensions as `not_recorded`, and never discards a denial merely because a class omits a file-oriented field.

Save the `spl` field as `linux_apparmor_denied`. Schedule it with a staggered cron such as `2-59/5 * * * *`; trigger when result count is greater than zero. The search dispatch reads `earliest=-10m@m latest=-5m@m`, a completed five-minute bucket delayed by five minutes for ingestion. Measure `_indextime-_time` on every source class. If p95 delivery lag exceeds five minutes, move both boundaries together and retest overlap/gaps; do not simply widen a recurring search and count the same denial repeatedly.

The base terms reduce the candidate set to the three documented deployment source types plus `apparmor` and `DENIED`. They are not the final decision. `rex` extracts the exact quoted decision from the event body, accepting either normal quotes or JSON-escaped quotes, and `where aa_decision="DENIED"` enforces the contract. Subsequent expressions extract common fields at search time. `stats` groups by stable triage dimensions, counts indexed denial records, calculates distinct audit IDs when present, and retains target names and audit IDs for drilldown. `distinct_audit_ids` is diagnostic only: missing IDs, source translation, or duplicated paths can make it differ from `denied_records`.

The initial threshold is any logged denial in the completed bucket. This is a sensitivity and evidence policy, not a vendor claim that one event is an incident. The former `count>5` delayed real low-frequency denials and had no cited source, traffic denominator, baseline, or service objective. Start with `severity=medium` ticket/report routing. Promote severity only through a local, tested policy that considers an exact profile/service, operation/class, target, recurrence, change state, and asset criticality. Do not infer criticality from operation names alone or add an undocumented universal count.

Do not use a CIM/tstats replacement unless the deployment creates a local normalized contract. No published accelerated CIM node represents AppArmor's decision, label/profile, mediation operation, masks, and audit serial together. Keep raw-event parity tests if local normalization is introduced.

## Step 3 — Validate source truth, SPL behavior, and mode handling

On a representative nonproduction host, run `aa-status` and capture the active profile/mode. Generate a narrowly scoped denied action using a disposable test profile and harmless test object under a written test plan. Do not probe `/etc/shadow`, production service paths, or dangerous capabilities merely because examples use them. Observe the same audit identity and key/value record with `ausearch` when auditd is present, or with `journalctl -k`/the chosen kernel log otherwise, then locate it in Splunk. Compare event time, host, decision, profile or label, operation, name, command, requested mask, denied mask, and audit ID exactly. Do not compare with a vendor UI: AppArmor has no administration UI that is a more authoritative comparator; `aa-status`, the selected on-host audit/kernel view, loaded profile source, and audit settings are the vendor-supported comparison surface. Document that fact instead of asserting an invented UI inventory count or percentage tolerance.

Execute the exact `controlTest` positive fixture in an isolated index with fixed search bounds first, then with times aligned to the scheduled closed bucket. Confirm every expected field and count. Repeat with two DENIED records with different audit serials and expect `denied_records=2` and `distinct_audit_ids=2`. Re-index an exact record through a second source path to demonstrate how duplicate architecture inflates the record count; remove the duplicate path rather than tuning the threshold.

Execute every negative variant. `apparmor="ALLOWED"` must not pass even when `denied_mask` is populated, because it is not the enforced-decision contract. Profile load/replace/remove messages and generic AVC/SYSCALL failures must not pass. Test `USER_AVC`/`type=1107` with `label` rather than `profile` and confirm normalization, but only when the record contains exact DENIED. Test absent optional fields and confirm `not_recorded`. Test lower-case or malformed decision strings and confirm rejection rather than silently normalizing an undocumented signature.

Validate time boundaries: a DENIED at the inclusive earliest boundary is in scope; one at the exclusive latest boundary is not. Confirm consecutive scheduled dispatches neither overlap nor leave a gap. Compare scheduler history with indexed event times and ingestion lag. Alert throttling can hide repeated notifications but does not correct overlapping windows, duplicate collection, or missing events. If throttling is used, key it on stable profile/host context and remember that Splunk documents alert edits as resetting throttle state.

Create a separate coverage report. Join an authoritative host/profile inventory to latest AppArmor source events and forwarder health; flag expected hosts with no recent events, audit/source status errors, unexpected source types, duplicate audit IDs across sources, and profiles unexpectedly in complain or unconfined state. Do not generate test denials continuously just to prove liveness. An empty detection search means no matching delivered record, not zero attempted violations and not healthy enforcement.

## Step 4 — Operationalize triage and evidence handling

For each finding, open the raw event before changing policy. Verify source/host identity and audit ID, then check current `aa-status`, the task's confinement where available, the loaded profile and local include, package/service revision, and same-time application error. Interpret fields by mediation class: `requested_mask` is what was requested and `denied_mask` identifies rejected permission bits in common file records; `name` can be an object path or another class-specific name; profile hats may appear in the profile label. Never assume every record names a file or that `comm` uniquely identifies an executable.

Classify the outcome as approved test, expected audited block, profile drift, legitimate new behavior needing a narrow rule, suspicious behavior, duplicate ingestion, or unresolved. If legitimate access is required, use normal AppArmor policy review: inspect the profile source/local include, add the least privilege rule, validate syntax, test in a controlled mode, obtain owner approval, reload through change management, and confirm both application behavior and disappearance of only the intended denial. Do not copy `name` and masks blindly into policy, run `aa-logprof` unattended, switch a fleet to complain mode, unload profiles, or disable AppArmor from an alert action.

For suspicious behavior, preserve the raw audit event and surrounding records, correlate process ancestry, executable/package integrity, authentication, service/network activity, and other endpoint evidence, and follow the incident-response plan. A denial proves the selected AppArmor check blocked an operation; it does not prove the preceding process was benign or malicious, that every stage was blocked, or that compromise failed. Conversely, a service error plus no denial does not exonerate AppArmor when logging or collection is incomplete.

Build the dashboard described in `visualization`. Keep coverage beside findings and separate enforced DENIED trends from any complain-mode ALLOWED learning report. A surge can indicate deployment drift or repeated hostile behavior, but volume alone is not a severity model. Route the initial medium finding to the profile/service owner and Linux security queue. Use case-management deduplication rather than broad SPL exclusions so every source record and scheduled result remains reviewable.

Retain evidence under the organization's approved security-log policy. Record kernel/AppArmor/tool versions, source path, add-on/forwarder version, effective configuration, profile hash and mode at observation, search revision, result, investigation, disposition, policy change, and suppression expiry. Object paths and process data may be sensitive; apply least privilege, integrity protection, and retention controls appropriate to host audit evidence. This catalogue entry supplies no evidence-signing or regulatory-satisfaction claim.

## Step 5 — Troubleshoot exact product-specific failure modes

- **No events in Splunk** — Confirm AppArmor is enabled and relevant profiles are loaded, then inspect the chosen on-host audit/kernel source. If the record exists there, check file permissions, journald stanza support, forwarder status, index routing, and effective `inputs.conf`. If it does not exist, review audit quieting, explicit deny behavior, auditd/backlog health, printk rate limiting, and profile coverage. Do not create a DENIED event on production solely for diagnosis.
- **On-host record exists but search misses it** — Search the raw event without source-type constraints, inspect actual `source`/`sourcetype`, and compare `MESSAGE` with `_raw`. Verify uppercase exact `apparmor="DENIED"`, quotation/JSON escaping, time parsing, index, and closed-window bounds. Update a qualified source contract only after retaining a sample and adding controls; do not broaden to bare `denied`.
- **`aa_profile=not_recorded`** — Check whether the class emits `label`, whether a structured transport truncated/escaped the message, and whether userspace mediation uses a different field shape. The raw DENIED remains valid evidence. Add a class-specific extraction only from authoritative samples and tests.
- **`distinct_audit_ids` is zero** — The source may omit or transform `audit(epoch:serial)`. Compare the raw on-host event and add-on translation. The rule still reports the denial, but audit-event deduplication and cross-record correlation are weaker; document that limitation.
- **Counts are doubled** — Group raw rows by host, audit ID, source, sourcetype, and forwarder. Disable overlapping audit-file/syslog/journald paths or duplicate stanzas. Do not divide counts by two or raise the threshold.
- **Only ALLOWED records appear** — Confirm the profile is in complain mode or audit/force-audit logging is active. This alert excludes them by design. Review profile readiness and use a separate learning workflow; do not relabel ALLOWED as DENIED or claim it was blocked.
- **Application failed but no DENIED appears** — Check ordinary DAC, seccomp, SELinux/other LSM stacking, filesystem, capability, resource, and application errors as well as AppArmor audit suppression/coverage. A generic failure is not an AppArmor denial without the exact record.
- **Alert repeats old findings** — Verify the saved search uses the closed non-overlapping bounds in the `spl` field and that `_time` is event time. Inspect scheduler dispatch arguments and lag. Throttling is notification control, not a substitute for correct windows.
- **Paths or commands look truncated** — Inspect line breaking, event truncation, JSON escaping, and raw source before changing rex. Preserve the complete event and qualify class-specific long records; truncation can remove decisive peer/target context.
- **Operators want automatic profile repair** — Keep remediation manual and change-controlled. A DENIED record does not establish that the requested access is safe, and automatic allow rules can erase the security boundary this detector is meant to observe.
grandmaExplanation: We watch when a Linux safety rule blocks a program from doing something it was not allowed to do. That helps the team tell the difference between a harmless software change, a broken rule, and behavior that needs a security investigation.
